transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in today?

Hello, Dr. Smith. I'm here because during long meetings at work, people will talk directly to me and I just completely zone out. I only realize afterward that I didn't actually hear a word they were saying, and it's starting to cause some real issues for me.
When you zone out, do you feel like you're spacing out or daydreaming, or does it feel more like you're suddenly not aware of your surroundings at all?

It definitely feels more like spacing out or daydreaming. I’m still fully aware of my surroundings and usually looking right at the person, but my mind has just drifted off to other thoughts, like what I'm going to make for dinner.
When you zone out, do these thoughts ever come back to you later as memories, or do you sometimes not remember anything about what happened during those moments?

I actually remember my own thoughts during those moments very clearly, like planning out a recipe or thinking about other tasks. But when it comes to what the speaker was saying to me, I have absolutely no memory of it because I just wasn't registering their words at all.
Do these zoning-out episodes happen more when you're feeling stressed or anxious, or do they also occur when you're feeling down, sad, or uninterested in things?

I'm not really sure, and I haven't really thought about whether my mood, like feeling sad or anxious, is connected to it. I just know that it happens a lot during those long meetings at work, regardless of how I'm feeling.
Do you feel anxious or worried before or during these meetings, even if you don’t think it’s related to the zoning out?

No, I don't really feel anxious or worried before or during the meetings. Instead, I get this intense physical restlessness, like a wired feeling where I just have this overwhelming urge to move or fidget. It's more about that physical need to get up than any kind of dread or anxiety.
Do you often have trouble staying seated when expected to, or do others describe you as constantly 'on the go' or acting as if 'driven by a motor'?

Yes, absolutely. During long meetings, sitting still feels so unbearable that I constantly find excuses to stand up, like refilling my water or grabbing printouts. My colleagues even joke that I can't sit still because I'm always pacing between my desk and the warehouse, and even at home, I'm constantly on the move reorganizing things instead of resting.
Have you often had these symptoms of restlessness and trouble staying seated since childhood, or did they start more recently in adulthood?

Actually, these issues go all the way back to childhood, and my elementary school teachers constantly wrote on my report cards that I couldn't sit still or wait my turn. While it's always been there, it really came to a head over the last couple of years since the restructuring at work. The transition to long, back-to-back meetings has made it much more noticeable and problematic.

In addition to the zoning out and restlessness, have you often had trouble paying attention, following through on instructions, or organizing tasks since childhood, not just at work but in school or daily life?

Even back in elementary school, the feedback was mainly about me being unable to sit still, talking over classmates, and getting sent to the hallway, rather than failing tests. In my current daily life, it really affects my relationship because I'm often too distracted to just sit and relax with my partner in the evenings.

Therefore, the candidate list remains unchanged.

The chronic nature, early onset, and functional impairment across settings support this diagnosis.
